title: Decision Models as L2 Rerankers for Content-Based Recommendation: A Pre-Registered Evaluation
content: In content-based recommendation, a second-stage (L2) reranker decides which of roughly a hundred retrieved items fill the first screen of results. The standard L2 model is a cross-encoder trained to score relevance. Decision models, general models that answer a typed question about a text with a probability, could offer an alternative through a single plain-language question. Whether they can is unknown: after retrieval most candidates are already on-topic, so the reranker must separate exact matches from close substitutes, a distinction decision models were not trained for, and sparse relevance labels make the comparison hard to measure. We cast a decision model as a pointwise reranker that asks, for each candidate, whether it exactly matches the request, and uses the answer probability as its score. We evaluate this under a pre-registered protocol: every model reranks the same frozen candidate lists, and a gain counts only if it holds both on the realistic retrieved lists and on fully labelled lists. On Amazon ESCI (1,000 requests) and Wayfair WANDS (299), the commercial Jev decision model, used zero-shot, improves P@10 over embedding order by 0.046 to 0.054 and significantly outperforms the Qwen3-Reranker cross-encoder on ESCI. The open decision model CLM-v0.1-8B ranks no better than random. Jev costs about four times more per request than the cross-encoder run on a rented cloud GPU, so the result is best read as evidence that some decision models can serve as high-precision L2 rerankers when accuracy at the top of the list matters more than serving cost.
